1	# Shot-logging app: plan
2	
3	Status: draft, updated with the owner's answers of October 27 (see "Decisions" at the end). Nothing here is
4	implemented. The design is in [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md) and the mockups
5	are in [mockups/](mockups/).
6	
7	Today a shot reaches the lake through the MCP server or the "Log a shot" issue form. Both work. Neither is pleasant
8	at the machine at 7am with a portafilter in one hand: the issue form is nine text fields, and the MCP route needs a
9	laptop or a chat. This plan describes a small phone web app that makes the common case (same coffee as yesterday,
10	small grind change) the timer plus three taps, and makes a new bag two taps: the photo and a confirm.
11	
12	## Goals
13	
14	- Log a repeat shot one-handed, without typing: start and stop the timer, then three taps.
15	- Start a new bag from a photo of it: read the roaster, coffee and roast date, match it to `dim_coffee`, confirm
16	  with one tap.
17	- Record equipment once (grinder, machine, basket) and have every shot point at the grinder it was ground on, so a
18	  grind setting means something across grinders.
19	- Show what a shot did the moment it's saved: ratio, time against the 25 to 32 s window, taste, and where it sits
20	  among this bag's shots. The app doesn't suggest grind changes yet (see Later: a dial-in model).
21	- Give each coffee a page with its shots, best recipe, and the catalog's current price and stock.
22	- Keep the lake append-only. New tables and new nullable columns only; every existing shot stays valid.
23	- Keep shots and bag photos private. Neither reaches the public tables, the public site or git. Shots come off
24	  the GitHub Pages site (see Privacy).
25	- Let the owner invite a few people. Each person has their own account, equipment, bags and shots, and sees only
26	  their own. Accounts are a username and a password, stored as salted hashes in a private Hugging Face dataset.
27	
28	## Non-goals
29	
30	- Open sign-up. People join only with an invite code from the owner. No sharing between accounts, no teams, and
31	  only two roles (owner, member).
32	- Shared machines. Nobody else pulls shots on the owner's machine; each account describes its own setup.
33	- Email. No addresses are collected, so there are no emails and no self-service password reset (see Accounts).
34	- A native app or an app store listing. A home-screen web app is enough.
35	- Bluetooth scales and machine integrations (Acaia, Decent, Gaggiuino). Chrome on Android does support Web
36	  Bluetooth, so a scale is possible later; for now typing two numbers is fine.
37	- Pour-over and filter recipes beyond what `brew_method` already stores. The UI is espresso-first.
38	- A reference per drink type. Lungo, Lance Hedrick's "soup" shot and pour-over such as V60 may later get their own;
39	  for now there's one window.
40	- Editing or deleting lake files. Corrections and retractions stay new records.
41	- Buying coffee. The coffee page links to the roaster's product page and stops there.
42	- Replacing the MCP server or the issue form. They keep working and gain the new fields where it's cheap.
43	
44	## User flows
45	
46	### 1. Capture a bag
47	
48	1. Today screen → "New bag". The camera opens (a file input with `capture="environment"`, which opens Android's
49	   camera without the app asking for camera permission).
50	2. Take the photo. The phone downsizes it to about 1600 px on the long edge and removes EXIF (GPS included) before
51	   upload.
52	3. The server sends the image to Claude with a fixed JSON schema: `roaster`, `coffee_name`, `roast_date`,
53	   `origin`, `process`, `weight_g`, plus a confidence per field. A typical read takes 2 to 5 s; the screen shows a
54	   skeleton of the match card meanwhile.
55	4. The server matches roaster first (against `dim_roaster` names and domains), then the coffee within that
56	   roaster's catalog, using `shots.fuzzy_match_coffee`'s scorer. Listed coffees rank above delisted ones.
57	5. A confident match uses the rule `shots.log_shot` already applies: the top score is at least 80 and at least 5
58	   ahead of the next one. The match card then shows the catalog title, roaster, origin, process, tasting notes,
59	   price per 100 g and stock, and the roast date that was read ("Oct 18 · day 9"). It shows no score; the
60	   number would only be noise when the answer is clear.
61	6. One tap on "Use this coffee" writes a `bags` record and opens the shot form. "Pick another match" opens the same
62	   list as a weak match.
63	7. A weak match (below 80, or two candidates within 5 points) skips the card. The sheet asks "Which one is it?",
64	   says what was read from the bag, and lists up to three candidates as rows, each with its score ("match 68") so
65	   the owner can see how close they are. Tapping a row picks it. "None of these: type the coffee" opens search; if
66	   nothing matches (a café bag, a roaster not in the registry), the bag is saved with free text, the same way
67	   `coffee_freetext` works today.
68	8. If the roast date couldn't be read, a date picker defaults to 7 days ago.
69	
70	Two taps when the match is confident, three when it's weak. The bag becomes the "current bag" until another one is started or it's marked
71	finished.
72	
73	### 2. Log a shot
74	
75	1. Today shows the current bag and a "Pull again" button with the last recipe ("18.0 → 36.4 g · grind 11").
76	2. "Pull again" opens the shot form prefilled from the last shot of this bag (or of this coffee, if the bag is
77	   new): dose, yield, grind, water temp, grinder, basket, brew method, milk drink. Time is not prefilled: it starts
78	   as "Not timed · last 29 s", because a copied time would be saved as if it were measured. The grind field shows
79	   the last shot's grind and nothing else; the app doesn't suggest a different one.
80	3. Adjust what changed with steppers (dose and yield in 0.1 g, time in 1 s, grind in the grinder's own step size).
81	   Time has two ways in, both always available: the built-in timer (Start when the pump starts, Stop when it
82	   stops) or typing it. "Type" opens a numeric keypad; tapping any numeral does the same for that field.
83	4. Pick taste (sour, balanced, bitter) and rating (1 to 5). Both start empty; they are the only new information in
84	   a repeat shot. A "Same as last" chip above them ("Same as last: balanced, 4") fills both in one tap when the shot
85	   tasted like yesterday's.
86	5. "Save shot". The saved screen shows the ratio, the time against the 25 to 32 s window, the taste, the shot's
87	   place on the dial-in target among this bag's shots, and one line comparing it with the last shot ("Inside the
88	   window, two seconds slower than Monday's shot"; "Ran fast at 22 s, outside the window"). It describes what
89	   happened and doesn't say what to change. "Undo" stays for 5 s. Undo writes a retraction record (`deleted: true`), not a delete.
90	
91	Repeat shot that tasted the same: Pull again, Start, Stop, "Same as last", Save. Three taps plus the timer. If the
92	taste or rating differs, it's taste and rating instead of "Same as last": four taps plus the timer. Saving without
93	a time turns the button into "Save with 29 s?". A second tap saves the last shot's time, recorded as copied
94	(`time_source` = `copied`), so it never passes for a measured time and the dial-in model leaves it out.
95	
96	### 3. Review a coffee
97	
98	From Today or from a bag in the history list: the coffee page. Header with the bag photo, roaster and coffee name,
99	origin, process and tasting notes from the catalog, plus current price per 100 g, stock and a link to the roaster.
100	Below: best recipe so far (one whole shot: highest rating, the latest of equal ratings, as `mart_dial_in` will pick
101	it; see dbt changes), a ratio-and-time chart of
102	every shot of this coffee coloured by taste, and the shot list. Each shot opens a read-only detail with "Correct"
103	(writes a new record with the same `shot_id`) and "Retract".
104	
105	### 4. Manage equipment
106	
107	Settings → Equipment. A list of grinders, machines and baskets. Each has a name and a few fields that matter for
108	the steppers and, later, the dial-in model: a grinder's scale (min, max, step) and which way is finer, a basket's nominal dose. One of each is marked
109	default. Adding a grinder takes a name and those three numbers. Retiring one hides it from pickers but keeps old
110	shots pointing at it. Changes are new records, with the latest per `equipment_id` winning.
111	
112	Most mornings nobody touches this screen. The shot form shows the current grinder and basket as one small chip
113	("DF64 V2 · Pullman 18 g"); tapping it switches.
114	
115	First run asks for a grinder (dial range, step, which way is finer) and a basket (nominal dose); nothing is
116	hard-coded. The owner's setup, entered then:
117	
118	| Kind | Name | Settings |
119	|---|---|---|
120	| Grinder | DF64 V2 | stepless dial, `scale_min` 0, `scale_max` 90, `finer_is_lower` true, stepper step entered at first run, default 0.5 |
121	| Machine | Lelit Bianca | default |
122	| Basket | Pullman Filtration Basket, 18 g | `model` = `basket17-pullm-v-v`, `basket_dose_g` 18 |
123	
124	The basket's 18 g becomes the default dose for a coffee's first shot.
125	
126	## Screens
127	
128	| Screen | Purpose | Mockup |
129	|---|---|---|
130	| Today | Current bag, "Pull again", last three shots, "New bag" | `mockups/today.html` |
131	| First run | No bag yet: photograph one, or add a grinder | `mockups/first-run.html` |
132	| Reading | The bag is being read: skeleton card, "Type the coffee" | `mockups/reading.html` |
133	| Match | Camera and a confident match | `mockups/capture.html` |
134	| Which one is it | A weak match: candidates with their scores | `mockups/match-weak.html` |
135	| Read failed | The label couldn't be read: Retake, or type the coffee | `mockups/read-failed.html` |
136	| Log shot | The prefilled form; the one screen that has to be fast | `mockups/log-shot.html` |
137	| Saved | Ratio, time against the window, taste, the target, a one-line comparison, undo | `mockups/saved.html` |
138	| Coffee | One coffee: catalog facts, best recipe, chart, shots | `mockups/coffee.html` |
139	| Setup | Equipment, plus the account: invite someone, sign out | `mockups/equipment.html` |
140	| Sign in | Username and password | `mockups/sign-in.html` |
141	| Sign up | Invite code, username, password | `mockups/sign-up.html` |
142	| Invite | Owner only: a new single-use code to send | `mockups/invite.html` |
143	| Search | Fallback when the photo match is wrong | not mocked; a search field over the match card list |
144	| History | All shots, newest first, grouped by bag | not mocked; same row component as Today |
145	
146	## Architecture
147	
148	### What has to be decided
149	
150	- Where the app runs, so the Hugging Face write token and the Anthropic key stay on a server.
151	- How people sign up and sign in, and where their accounts live.
152	- How a shot gets from the phone into the lake.
153	- Where the bag photo is read.
154	- What happens with no network.
155	
156	### Hosting
157	
158	Decided by the owner: Google Cloud Run in `us-central1`, managed with Terraform in `src/terraform/`. The data stays on
159	Hugging Face; only the app moves. This continues the original repo's GCP and Terraform lineage.
160	
161	| Option | For | Against |
162	|---|---|---|
163	| A. Hugging Face Space (Docker) | Same account as the lake. | Docker Spaces need an HF PRO subscription, even on free CPU (creating one in #15 returned 402). |
164	| B. Cloudflare Workers + Pages | Never sleeps, free at this volume. | JavaScript: matching and the Parquet writer would be a second implementation that drifts from the Python one. |
165	| C. Google Cloud Run (chosen) | Runs the Docker image #15 already built, so `coffeedata`'s matching and lake writer are reused, not rewritten. Scales to zero, Secret Manager for keys, keyless deploys from GitHub, and Terraform for everything. | A Google Cloud project and billing account to look after. |
166	| D. No server: static app that opens GitHub issues | Reuses the issue-form workflow. | A GitHub token on the phone, a minute per shot through Actions, no photos and no saved summary. |
167	
168	What Terraform in `src/terraform/` manages:
169	
170	- The Cloud Run service in `us-central1`, running as its own service account, with the image from an Artifact
171	  Registry repository.
172	- Secret Manager secrets for `HF_TOKEN`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `AUTH_PEPPER`, `SESSION_SECRET` and
173	  `OWNER_SETUP_CODE`, exposed to the service as environment variables. Terraform creates the secrets and grants
174	  access; the values are added outside it (`gcloud secrets versions add`), so they never sit in Terraform state.
175	- The domain mapping for `app.registry.coffee` (see Domain).
176	- Workload Identity Federation for GitHub Actions: a pool and provider that trust this repo's workflows, and a deploy
177	  service account they can impersonate. Deploys need no JSON key. A workflow on pushes to `main` that touch `app/`
178	  or `src/` builds the image, pushes it to Artifact Registry and deploys a new revision.
179	- A budget of $5 a month on the project, with alert emails at 50%, 90% and 100%. A budget only warns; it doesn't
180	  stop spending. Max instances 1 is what keeps a runaway bill unlikely.
181	- Terraform's own state lives in a GCS bucket, created once before the first `terraform apply`.
182	
183	How the app runs there:
184	
185	- Min instances 0 to start. The first request after an idle spell waits for a cold start (a few seconds for this
186	  image); the owner accepted cold starts. Raising it to 1 is a one-line change if that starts to annoy.
187	- Max instances 1. The server keeps shots, bags, equipment, the sign-in lockout counters and the write lock in
188	  memory, and assumes it's the only writer. A second instance would have its own copy and its own lock, so the
189	  service must never scale past one. One instance serves many requests at once, which is plenty here.
190	- By default Cloud Run gives an instance CPU only while a request is in flight. The app already finishes every
191	  lake commit before it answers, so nothing runs after a response.
192	- The filesystem is in memory and goes away with the instance, like a Space's disk. Nothing waits in staging: each
193	  write is published before it's acknowledged, and the phone's outbox holds it until then (see Offline). Staged
194	  files count against the instance's memory, so the service gets 1 GiB.
195	
196	The original proposal had a Space; the parts of it that mattered carry over. The tokens stay on the server, and the
197	server keeps an in-memory copy of shots, bags and equipment, updated on every write, because reading one file per
198	shot over `hf://` is one HTTP request per file. At start, shots come from the weekly `marts/fct_shot.parquet`
199	export, which keeps each shot's own columns (`shot_coffee_id` and so on, beside the values `fct_shot` fills in from
200	the bag) and `logged_at` (#15). Then every shot file written since the export's snapshot began is read on top,
201	latest wins. The export records `snapshot_at`, the time dbt started reading shots, and the seed reads files from
202	that time on, not just files newer than the latest `logged_at` in the export: a file staged before the snapshot but
203	published after it would otherwise be missed. Bags and equipment are few, so they're read straight from their
204	files. With no export yet, the server reads every shot file.
205	
206	### Domain: registry.coffee
207	
208	The owner is buying back `registry.coffee`. The name fits: the catalog is a registry of US roasters and their
209	coffees, and the lake already has a `registry` table. The addresses are decided:
210	
211	- `registry.coffee`: the public launch page, built by GitHub Pages (#19), with the catalog dashboard at
212	  `registry.coffee/catalog/`. Pages supports a custom apex domain with HTTPS for free; it needs the A/AAAA records
213	  and a `CNAME` file in the site output.
214	- `app.registry.coffee`: the shot-logging app on Cloud Run, through a Cloud Run domain mapping. Set up in this
215	  order:
216	  1. Verify `registry.coffee` in Google Search Console (a TXT record at Namecheap).
217	  2. Add a CAA record at Namecheap allowing `pki.goog`, so Google can issue the certificate. Without it, a CAA
218	     record that names only another authority would block issuance.
219	  3. Create the domain mapping (in Terraform).
220	  4. Add the CNAME `app` → `ghs.googlehosted.com` at Namecheap. Google then issues the certificate, which can take
221	     a while after DNS settles.
222	
223	  If domain mappings ever fall short (they're region-limited, and `us-central1` has them), a global
224	  external HTTPS load balancer in front of the service does the same job, in the same Terraform.
225	
226	The session cookie is host-only on `app.registry.coffee`, apart from the public site, and links in invites use that
227	address.
228	
229	### Accounts and sign-in
230	
231	The owner asked for a simple sign-up and login of our own, with the hashed credentials kept in a Hugging Face
232	dataset, instead of "Sign in with Hugging Face" (most invitees won't have an HF account). So:
233	
234	#### Where accounts live
235	
236	A third private dataset, `hf://datasets/jtouley/coffee-data-users`, holding two
237	append-only tables, `users` and `invites` (see Data model). Keeping accounts apart from the lake and the photos
238	means nothing that reads the lake (dbt, the MCP server, the weekly run) can see a password hash, and the token
239	the weekly run uses doesn't need access to it. The server loads both tables into memory at start and writes a new
240	record (one commit) for every change.
241	
242	#### Passwords
243	
244	Hashed with Argon2id (`argon2-cffi`, its default RFC 9106 low-memory parameters: 64 MiB, 3 passes,
245	4 lanes), with a per-hash random salt. Before hashing, the password is HMAC-ed with a pepper kept in Secret Manager
246	(`AUTH_PEPPER`), so a copy of the users dataset alone isn't enough to start guessing. Rules follow NIST 800-63B:
247	at least 10 characters, no composition rules, and a check against a short list of common passwords. Changing a
248	password writes a new `users` record.
249	
250	#### Sign-up
251	
252	Only with an invite code.
253	
254	1. The owner taps "Invite someone" and gets a code like `K7QD-M2XF-9RPA-T4WE`: 80 random bits as 16 characters of Crockford base32 (digits
255	   and capitals without I, L, O and U; on input O reads as 0, I and L as 1, case and dashes don't matter), valid for
256	   7 days and usable once, and a link, `app.registry.coffee/join#K7QD-M2XF-9RPA-T4WE`. "Share link" opens
257	   Android's share sheet. Only the code's SHA-256 is stored, so it can't be shown again later; a pending invite
258	   offers "Send a new link", which revokes the old code and makes a new one. The code sits after `#`, so it never
259	   reaches server logs as part of the URL.
260	2. The invitee opens the link, lands on "jtouley invited you" with the code filled in, picks a username and a
261	   password, and is signed in. Typing the code by hand also works.
262	3. Bootstrapping the owner: when the `users` table is empty, the first sign-up needs `OWNER_SETUP_CODE`, a secret in
263	   Secret Manager, and creates the `owner` account. Each value of the secret works once: the server stores the SHA-256 of
264	   every setup code it has accepted, in the users dataset, and refuses a value it has seen. A setup code that has
265	   been used is inert, so leaving it in Secret Manager is no standing way into the owner's account.
266	
267	#### Sign-in
268	
269	Username and password. A failed attempt gets the same message whether the username exists or not, and
270	an unknown username is still checked against a dummy hash so the timing doesn't tell. Usernames are visible to
271	anyone who has been invited, so a lockout keyed on the username alone would let anyone keep the owner locked out.
272	Instead:
273	
274	- Five failures for one username from one IP lock that pair for 15 minutes.
275	- Twenty failures from one IP lock that IP for 15 minutes.
276	- Failures for one username across all IPs only slow it down: each one doubles a delay before the next attempt is
277	  checked, from 1 s up to 30 s. They never lock it.
278	
279	All of this is kept in memory; a restart clears it, which is acceptable at this size.
280	
281	#### Sessions
282	
283	No session table in the dataset (that would be a commit per login). The cookie is a signed token
284	(HMAC-SHA256 with the `SESSION_SECRET` secret) carrying `user_id`, `session_epoch` and the issue time. It is
285	`HttpOnly`, `Secure` and `SameSite=Lax`, lasts 90 days, and renews itself on use. Each `users` record has a
286	`session_epoch`. "Sign out everywhere", a password change and the owner disabling an account all bump it, which
287	invalidates every older cookie. Writes also need an `X-Requested-With` header, which a cross-site form can't send,
288	as CSRF protection on top of `SameSite`.
289	
290	#### Forgotten passwords
291	
292	There's no email, so the owner issues a reset code from the Invite screen. It works like an
293	invite but is tied to an existing account, and using it sets a new password and bumps the epoch. To reset the
294	owner's own password, the owner adds a new version of the `OWNER_SETUP_CODE` secret in Secret Manager (which proves
295	control of the Google Cloud project) and uses it once on the reset screen; as with setup, a value that has been used never works again.
296	
297	#### Every request is scoped
298	
299	Every write needs a signed-in account and touches only that account's data. The server reads `user_id` from the
300	cookie, never from the request body, and filters every read and write by it. The in-memory caches are keyed by
301	user. Tests cover a request with no session, or an expired or tampered one, trying each write route (rejected with
302	nothing written), and one user trying to read, correct or retract another user's shot, bag, photo or equipment.
303	
304	Rejected: Sign in with Hugging Face (invitees would need HF accounts), Identity-Aware Proxy in front of Cloud Run (invitees would need Google accounts), passkeys only
305	(good, but more code to get right; worth adding later as a second way in), and magic links (need email).
306	
307	### How writes reach the lake
308	
309	Each action is one Hugging Face commit, made by the server with the existing `Lake.write` and `Lake.publish`:
310	
311	- Sign-up, password change, invite: one commit each to the users dataset.
312	- New bag: two commits. First the photo's Parquet file to the photo dataset, then the `bags` row to the lake. If
313	  the second fails, the photo is orphaned but harmless, and the outbox retries the bag.
314	- Shot: one `shots` file.
315	- Equipment change: one `equipment` file.
316	
317	`Lake.publish` already retries with backoff and treats files that landed on a lost response as uploaded. A commit
318	takes a second or two. The phone shows the saved screen immediately (the summary needs only the shot and data the server
319	already holds) and marks the shot as synced when the commit returns.
320	
321	The phone generates `shot_id` and `bag_id` (UUIDs) before sending, and keeps each write in its outbox until the
322	server acknowledges it. The outbox sends a user's entries one at a time, in the order they were made. Three rules
323	keep retries from undoing anything:
324	
325	- Every record carries `rev`, a counter the phone sets to one more than the `rev` of the version it last saw (1 for a
326	  new record). The server drops a write whose `rev` isn't greater than the stored one. So a save whose response was
327	  lost, resent after an Undo or a Correct, can't bring the old version back. `logged_at` is still stamped by the
328	  server, but it no longer decides between two versions from the phone.
329	- A resend identical to what's stored is acknowledged without writing (#13).
330	- File names are `<id>__<logged_at>-<6 random hex>.parquet` for every table, so two records for one id in the same
331	  second never collide. #13 does this for shots; equipment and bags need the suffix too (#22).
332	
333	Each dataset (lake, photos, users) has its own staging folder (`build/lake-staging`, `build/photos-staging`,
334	`build/users-staging`), and `Lake.publish` uploads only that dataset's folder, one publish at a time per dataset,
335	under a lock. A shot publish can't carry a password hash or a photo into the main lake. A file that went up in
336	another request's commit counts as published, so a request never retries a commit that already succeeded.
337	
338	The weekly run and the app can commit to the dataset at the same time: they touch different paths, and the
339	`concurrency: lake` group in Actions doesn't cover the app, so this relies on HF commits not conflicting on
340	disjoint files. The owner has approved one test during milestone 2: a commit from a test deployment to a test path
341	while a weekly run is committing.

343	### Where the bag photo is read
344	
345	On the server, with the Anthropic key in Secret Manager. One request per photo: the image, a short instruction and
346	a JSON schema through structured outputs, so the response always parses. Bag labels are short but varied
347	(hand-lettered names, stickers on kraft paper, dates as "R 10.18" or "Roasted on 18/10").
348	
349	The model is chosen by measurement, as the owner asked: Claude Opus 5.5 (`claude-opus-5-5`) and Claude Haiku 5.5
350	(`claude-haiku-5-5`) are compared on the same set of real bags before either becomes the default.
351	
352	- The set: real bag photos with the right answer attached. The app builds this as it's used: every bag confirmed
353	  on the match card (or corrected through "Pick another match") is a photo with a known `coffee_id` and roast date. The
354	  first comparison runs on whatever bags exist when capture ships, plus any old bags or photos the owner has to
355	  hand, and it's re-run once there are 20. Hard labels (hand lettering, a sticker on kraft paper, a date stamp, a
356	  café's own bag) are worth adding on purpose.
357	- Until the comparison has 20 bags, Opus is the default, since it's the safer reader and costs about a cent a bag.
358	- Each model reads every photo three times at low effort, with the same prompt and schema.
359	- Scored per field: roaster, coffee name and roast date exact (after normalizing case and date format), plus the
360	  end-to-end result that matters: did the Python matcher land on the right `coffee_id`? Also logged: latency and
361	  cost per read, and whether the three runs agreed.
362	- Rule: use Haiku if it gets the same number of correct end-to-end matches as Opus (or misses only bags that Opus
363	  also struggles with) and its median latency is lower. Otherwise use Opus; at one bag a week the cost difference
364	  is under a dollar a year, so accuracy decides.
365	- The comparison is a script in the repo (`app/eval/bag_read.py`) with the photos in the private photo dataset, so
366	  it can be re-run whenever the prompt or the models change.

368	With Opus, the request turns on the API's server-side refusal fallback, so a declined read falls back to another
369	model instead of failing. Haiku 5.5 has no server-side fallback, so with Haiku a declined or failed read drops to

372	The model only reads the label. Matching to the catalog stays deterministic, in Python, against `dim_coffee`; the
373	model never sees the catalog. That keeps the read cheap and the matching testable.

375	Rejected: reading on the phone (on-device OCR gets the text but not "which of these words is the roaster"), and

378	### Offline
379	
380	Kitchen Wi-Fi is usually fine, but a shot should never be lost to a dropped connection.
381	
382	- The app is a PWA with a service worker that caches the shell, so it opens offline.
383	- Every write goes through an outbox in IndexedDB and is retried until the server acknowledges the commit. The
384	  Today screen shows a small "2 waiting to sync" line when the outbox isn't empty. What each answer does to an
385	  entry:
386	  - 2xx: the entry is removed. This is the only answer that removes one silently.
387	  - No answer (offline, timeout, dropped connection), 408, 429 and any 5xx: the entry stays and is retried with
388	    backoff (from 2 s, doubling, up to 5 minutes), honouring `Retry-After` when the server sends it.
389	  - 401: the entry stays, and the app asks the person to sign in again; it's sent once they have.
390	  - Any other 4xx (the write can never succeed as sent, such as 400, 403, 404, 409 for a stale `rev`, or 422):
391	    the entry moves to a "Couldn't save" list on Today, with the server's message, where it can be fixed and resent
392	    or discarded by hand. It's never dropped without the person seeing it.
393	- Offline, the form still prefills from the locally cached last shots, and the saved screen draws its summary and
394	  target from them. That summary (the ratio, the window check, the difference from the last shot) is the one piece
395	  of the server's logic repeated in the browser. It's a few lines, kept in step with the Python version by shared
396	  test cases.
397	- Bag capture needs the network (the photo has to be read). Offline, "New bag" saves the photo to the outbox and
398	  lets the owner type the coffee or pick a recent one; the read and match happen when it syncs.

555	## Privacy
556	
557	- Bag photos stay private. They go to a separate private dataset, `hf://datasets/jtouley/coffee-data-photos`, as
558	  Parquet files in Hugging Face's `Image` layout, one photo per file. The main lake is private too, but a separate dataset means a
559	  mistake in the public export can't reach a photo, and the photos could be deleted wholesale without touching the
560	  lake's history. Only the `photo_id` is in the main lake.
561	- Why Parquet and not plain JPEG files: a Parquet photo goes through the same `Lake.write` and `Lake.publish` as every
562	  other record, and the image and its metadata (who, when, size, hash) are one immutable file that can't drift apart.
563	  Plain JPEGs would need a second write path for binary files and a separate metadata table kept in step with them.
564	- EXIF is removed on the phone before upload, so GPS coordinates of the kitchen never leave it. The server
565	  re-encodes the JPEG as a second check before writing the bytes into Parquet.
566	- Photos are served only through the app, to the user who took them, never by a direct HF URL. The server reads
567	  the `image` column and returns the bytes.
568	- Invited people's data lives in the owner's private datasets, so the owner can read it. The sign-up screen says so
569	  in one sentence. The app itself never shows one user another's data.
570	- Leaving. Retracting records hides them in the app and in dbt, but the lake is append-only and HF keeps file
571	  history, so a retraction isn't erasure. If an invitee asks for their data to be erased, the owner deletes their
572	  files from the three datasets and squashes the history (`HfApi.super_squash_history`). It's a manual
573	  exception to append-only, and it's the reason accounts and photos live in their own datasets: erasing them doesn't
574	  rewrite the catalog's history.
575	- Passwords never leave the server in plain text and are never logged. Request logging drops the body of the
576	  sign-in, sign-up and reset routes.
577	- The image goes to the Anthropic API to be read. Under standard API terms it isn't used for training; it is still
578	  a third party seeing a photo of a kitchen counter. The capture screen frames the bag tightly to keep the
579	  background small.
580	- Shots leave the public site. Today `site.py` renders "My shots: rating by brew ratio" and "Recent shots" from
581	  `fct_shot` on the GitHub Pages site; milestone 1 removes both sections and the scatter chart, and adds a test
582	  that the generated site contains no shot fields. Shots are then visible only in the app.
583	- The "Log a shot" issue form posts the shot and the reply as a GitHub issue, which is public if the repo is. #15
584	  kept it, since `suggest_next` still serves its replies. It stays until the app is live; then it comes off `main` and
585	  is kept on an archive branch, never deleted.

649	## Later: a dial-in model
650	
651	The app doesn't suggest grind changes. The current rule ("sour or fast, go finer") is a rule of thumb, not something
652	learned from these shots, and a confident-looking suggestion from it would be wrong often enough to mislead. The
653	data the app collects is what a better suggestion needs: grind, dose, yield, time, taste, rating, grinder and the
654	bag's roast date.

656	Once a coffee has enough shots on one grinder (about 20), fit a small per-bag model of time and taste against grind,
657	dose and days off roast; a regression with a term per bag is enough to start. Compare it with the rule of thumb on
658	held-out shots: for each held-out shot, which one better predicted the time and taste of the next one? Show a
659	suggestion in the app only when the model reports its confidence and beats the rule of thumb on that test, and say
660	how sure it is ("Try 11. Likely 26 to 30 s.") instead of stating a single answer.

# Shot-logging app: plan

Status: draft, updated with the owner's answers of October 27 (see "Decisions" at the end). Nothing here is
implemented. The design is in [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md) and the mockups
are in [mockups/](mockups/).

Today a shot reaches the lake through the MCP server or the "Log a shot" issue form. Both work. Neither is pleasant
at the machine at 7am with a portafilter in one hand: the issue form is nine text fields, and the MCP route needs a
laptop or a chat. This plan describes a small phone web app that makes the common case (same coffee as yesterday,
small grind change) the timer plus three taps, and makes a new bag two taps: the photo and a confirm.

## Goals

- Log a repeat shot one-handed, without typing: start and stop the timer, then three taps.
- Start a new bag from a photo of it: read the roaster, coffee and roast date, match it to `dim_coffee`, confirm
  with one tap.
- Record equipment once (grinder, machine, basket) and have every shot point at the grinder it was ground on, so a
  grind setting means something across grinders.
- Show what a shot did the moment it's saved: ratio, time against the 25 to 32 s window, taste, and where it sits
  among this bag's shots. The app doesn't suggest grind changes yet (see Later: a dial-in model).
- Give each coffee a page with its shots, best recipe, and the catalog's current price and stock.
- Keep the lake append-only. New tables and new nullable columns only; every existing shot stays valid.
- Keep shots and bag photos private. Neither reaches the public tables, the public site or git. Shots come off
  the GitHub Pages site (see Privacy).
- Let the owner invite a few people. Each person has their own account, equipment, bags and shots, and sees only
  their own. Accounts are a username and a password, stored as salted hashes in a private Hugging Face dataset.

## Non-goals

- Open sign-up. People join only with an invite code from the owner. No sharing between accounts, no teams, and
  only two roles (owner, member).
- Shared machines. Nobody else pulls shots on the owner's machine; each account describes its own setup.
- Email. No addresses are collected, so there are no emails and no self-service password reset (see Accounts).
- A native app or an app store listing. A home-screen web app is enough.
- Bluetooth scales and machine integrations (Acaia, Decent, Gaggiuino). Chrome on Android does support Web
  Bluetooth, so a scale is possible later; for now typing two numbers is fine.
- Pour-over and filter recipes beyond what `brew_method` already stores. The UI is espresso-first.
- A reference per drink type. Lungo, Lance Hedrick's "soup" shot and pour-over such as V60 may later get their own;
  for now there's one window.
- Editing or deleting lake files. Corrections and retractions stay new records.
- Buying coffee. The coffee page links to the roaster's product page and stops there.
- Replacing the MCP server or the issue form. They keep working and gain the new fields where it's cheap.

## User flows

### 1. Capture a bag

1. Today screen → "New bag". The camera opens (a file input with `capture="environment"`, which opens Android's
   camera without the app asking for camera permission).
2. Take the photo. The phone downsizes it to about 1600 px on the long edge and removes EXIF (GPS included) before
   upload.
3. The server sends the image to Claude with a fixed JSON schema: `roaster`, `coffee_name`, `roast_date`,
   `origin`, `process`, `weight_g`, plus a confidence per field. A typical read takes 2 to 5 s; the screen shows a
   skeleton of the match card meanwhile.
4. The server matches roaster first (against `dim_roaster` names and domains), then the coffee within that
   roaster's catalog, using `shots.fuzzy_match_coffee`'s scorer. Listed coffees rank above delisted ones.
5. A confident match uses the rule `shots.log_shot` already applies: the top score is at least 80 and at least 5
   ahead of the next one. The match card then shows the catalog title, roaster, origin, process, tasting notes,
   price per 100 g and stock, and the roast date that was read ("Oct 18 · day 9"). It shows no score; the
   number would only be noise when the answer is clear.
6. One tap on "Use this coffee" writes a `bags` record and opens the shot form. "Pick another match" opens the same
   list as a weak match.
7. A weak match (below 80, or two candidates within 5 points) skips the card. The sheet asks "Which one is it?",
   says what was read from the bag, and lists up to three candidates as rows, each with its score ("match 68") so
   the owner can see how close they are. Tapping a row picks it. "None of these: type the coffee" opens search; if
   nothing matches (a café bag, a roaster not in the registry), the bag is saved with free text, the same way
   `coffee_freetext` works today.
8. If the roast date couldn't be read, a date picker defaults to 7 days ago.

Two taps when the match is confident, three when it's weak. The bag becomes the "current bag" until another one is started or it's marked
finished.

### 2. Log a shot

1. Today shows the current bag and a "Pull again" button with the last recipe ("18.0 → 36.4 g · grind 11").
2. "Pull again" opens the shot form prefilled from the last shot of this bag (or of this coffee, if the bag is
   new): dose, yield, grind, water temp, grinder, basket, brew method, milk drink. Time is not prefilled: it starts
   as "Not timed · last 29 s", because a copied time would be saved as if it were measured. The grind field shows
   the last shot's grind and nothing else; the app doesn't suggest a different one.
3. Adjust what changed with steppers (dose and yield in 0.1 g, time in 1 s, grind in the grinder's own step size).
   Time has two ways in, both always available: the built-in timer (Start when the pump starts, Stop when it
   stops) or typing it. "Type" opens a numeric keypad; tapping any numeral does the same for that field.
4. Pick taste (sour, balanced, bitter) and rating (1 to 5). Both start empty; they are the only new information in
   a repeat shot. A "Same as last" chip above them ("Same as last: balanced, 4") fills both in one tap when the shot
   tasted like yesterday's.
5. "Save shot". The saved screen shows the ratio, the time against the 25 to 32 s window, the taste, the shot's
   place on the dial-in target among this bag's shots, and one line comparing it with the last shot ("Inside the
   window, two seconds slower than Monday's shot"; "Ran fast at 22 s, outside the window"). It describes what
   happened and doesn't say what to change. "Undo" stays for 5 s. Undo writes a retraction record (`deleted: true`), not a delete.

Repeat shot that tasted the same: Pull again, Start, Stop, "Same as last", Save. Three taps plus the timer. If the
taste or rating differs, it's taste and rating instead of "Same as last": four taps plus the timer. Saving without
a time turns the button into "Save with 29 s?". A second tap saves the last shot's time, recorded as copied
(`time_source` = `copied`), so it never passes for a measured time and the dial-in model leaves it out.

### 3. Review a coffee

From Today or from a bag in the history list: the coffee page. Header with the bag photo, roaster and coffee name,
origin, process and tasting notes from the catalog, plus current price per 100 g, stock and a link to the roaster.
Below: best recipe so far (one whole shot: highest rating, the latest of equal ratings, as `mart_dial_in` will pick
it; see dbt changes), a ratio-and-time chart of
every shot of this coffee coloured by taste, and the shot list. Each shot opens a read-only detail with "Correct"
(writes a new record with the same `shot_id`) and "Retract".

### 4. Manage equipment

Settings → Equipment. A list of grinders, machines and baskets. Each has a name and a few fields that matter for
the steppers and, later, the dial-in model: a grinder's scale (min, max, step) and which way is finer, a basket's nominal dose. One of each is marked
default. Adding a grinder takes a name and those three numbers. Retiring one hides it from pickers but keeps old
shots pointing at it. Changes are new records, with the latest per `equipment_id` winning.

Most mornings nobody touches this screen. The shot form shows the current grinder and basket as one small chip
("DF64 V2 · Pullman 18 g"); tapping it switches.

First run asks for a grinder (dial range, step, which way is finer) and a basket (nominal dose); nothing is
hard-coded. The owner's setup, entered then:

| Kind | Name | Settings |
|---|---|---|
| Grinder | DF64 V2 | stepless dial, `scale_min` 0, `scale_max` 90, `finer_is_lower` true, stepper step entered at first run, default 0.5 |
| Machine | Lelit Bianca | default |
| Basket | Pullman Filtration Basket, 18 g | `model` = `basket17-pullm-v-v`, `basket_dose_g` 18 |

The basket's 18 g becomes the default dose for a coffee's first shot.

## Screens

| Screen | Purpose | Mockup |
|---|---|---|
| Today | Current bag, "Pull again", last three shots, "New bag" | `mockups/today.html` |
| First run | No bag yet: photograph one, or add a grinder | `mockups/first-run.html` |
| Reading | The bag is being read: skeleton card, "Type the coffee" | `mockups/reading.html` |
| Match | Camera and a confident match | `mockups/capture.html` |
| Which one is it | A weak match: candidates with their scores | `mockups/match-weak.html` |
| Read failed | The label couldn't be read: Retake, or type the coffee | `mockups/read-failed.html` |
| Log shot | The prefilled form; the one screen that has to be fast | `mockups/log-shot.html` |
| Saved | Ratio, time against the window, taste, the target, a one-line comparison, undo | `mockups/saved.html` |
| Coffee | One coffee: catalog facts, best recipe, chart, shots | `mockups/coffee.html` |
| Setup | Equipment, plus the account: invite someone, sign out | `mockups/equipment.html` |
| Sign in | Username and password | `mockups/sign-in.html` |
| Sign up | Invite code, username, password | `mockups/sign-up.html` |
| Invite | Owner only: a new single-use code to send | `mockups/invite.html` |
| Search | Fallback when the photo match is wrong | not mocked; a search field over the match card list |
| History | All shots, newest first, grouped by bag | not mocked; same row component as Today |

## Architecture

### What has to be decided

- Where the app runs, so the Hugging Face write token and the Anthropic key stay on a server.
- How people sign up and sign in, and where their accounts live.
- How a shot gets from the phone into the lake.
- Where the bag photo is read.
- What happens with no network.

### Hosting

Decided by the owner: Google Cloud Run in `us-central1`, managed with Terraform in `src/terraform/`. The data stays on
Hugging Face; only the app moves. This continues the original repo's GCP and Terraform lineage.

| Option | For | Against |
|---|---|---|
| A. Hugging Face Space (Docker) | Same account as the lake. | Docker Spaces need an HF PRO subscription, even on free CPU (creating one in #15 returned 402). |
| B. Cloudflare Workers + Pages | Never sleeps, free at this volume. | JavaScript: matching and the Parquet writer would be a second implementation that drifts from the Python one. |
| C. Google Cloud Run (chosen) | Runs the Docker image #15 already built, so `coffeedata`'s matching and lake writer are reused, not rewritten. Scales to zero, Secret Manager for keys, keyless deploys from GitHub, and Terraform for everything. | A Google Cloud project and billing account to look after. |
| D. No server: static app that opens GitHub issues | Reuses the issue-form workflow. | A GitHub token on the phone, a minute per shot through Actions, no photos and no saved summary. |

What Terraform in `src/terraform/` manages:

- The Cloud Run service in `us-central1`, running as its own service account, with the image from an Artifact
  Registry repository.
- Secret Manager secrets for `HF_TOKEN`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `AUTH_PEPPER`, `SESSION_SECRET` and
  `OWNER_SETUP_CODE`, exposed to the service as environment variables. Terraform creates the secrets and grants
  access; the values are added outside it (`gcloud secrets versions add`), so they never sit in Terraform state.
- The domain mapping for `app.registry.coffee` (see Domain).
- Workload Identity Federation for GitHub Actions: a pool and provider that trust this repo's workflows, and a deploy
  service account they can impersonate. Deploys need no JSON key. A workflow on pushes to `main` that touch `app/`
  or `src/` builds the image, pushes it to Artifact Registry and deploys a new revision.
- A budget of $5 a month on the project, with alert emails at 50%, 90% and 100%. A budget only warns; it doesn't
  stop spending. Max instances 1 is what keeps a runaway bill unlikely.
- Terraform's own state lives in a GCS bucket, created once before the first `terraform apply`.

How the app runs there:

- Min instances 0 to start. The first request after an idle spell waits for a cold start (a few seconds for this
  image); the owner accepted cold starts. Raising it to 1 is a one-line change if that starts to annoy.
- Max instances 1. The server keeps shots, bags, equipment, the sign-in lockout counters and the write lock in
  memory, and assumes it's the only writer. A second instance would have its own copy and its own lock, so the
  service must never scale past one. One instance serves many requests at once, which is plenty here.
- By default Cloud Run gives an instance CPU only while a request is in flight. The app already finishes every
  lake commit before it answers, so nothing runs after a response.
- The filesystem is in memory and goes away with the instance, like a Space's disk. Nothing waits in staging: each
  write is published before it's acknowledged, and the phone's outbox holds it until then (see Offline). Staged
  files count against the instance's memory, so the service gets 1 GiB.

The original proposal had a Space; the parts of it that mattered carry over. The tokens stay on the server, and the
server keeps an in-memory copy of shots, bags and equipment, updated on every write, because reading one file per
shot over `hf://` is one HTTP request per file. At start, shots come from the weekly `marts/fct_shot.parquet`
export, which keeps each shot's own columns (`shot_coffee_id` and so on, beside the values `fct_shot` fills in from
the bag) and `logged_at` (#15). Then every shot file written since the export's snapshot began is read on top,
latest wins. The export records `snapshot_at`, the time dbt started reading shots, and the seed reads files from
that time on, not just files newer than the latest `logged_at` in the export: a file staged before the snapshot but
published after it would otherwise be missed. Bags and equipment are few, so they're read straight from their
files. With no export yet, the server reads every shot file.

### Domain: registry.coffee

The owner is buying back `registry.coffee`. The name fits: the catalog is a registry of US roasters and their
coffees, and the lake already has a `registry` table. The addresses are decided:

- `registry.coffee`: the public launch page, built by GitHub Pages (#19), with the catalog dashboard at
  `registry.coffee/catalog/`. Pages supports a custom apex domain with HTTPS for free; it needs the A/AAAA records
  and a `CNAME` file in the site output.
- `app.registry.coffee`: the shot-logging app on Cloud Run, through a Cloud Run domain mapping. Set up in this
  order:
  1. Verify `registry.coffee` in Google Search Console (a TXT record at Namecheap).
  2. Add a CAA record at Namecheap allowing `pki.goog`, so Google can issue the certificate. Without it, a CAA
     record that names only another authority would block issuance.
  3. Create the domain mapping (in Terraform).
  4. Add the CNAME `app` → `ghs.googlehosted.com` at Namecheap. Google then issues the certificate, which can take
     a while after DNS settles.

  If domain mappings ever fall short (they're region-limited, and `us-central1` has them), a global
  external HTTPS load balancer in front of the service does the same job, in the same Terraform.

The session cookie is host-only on `app.registry.coffee`, apart from the public site, and links in invites use that
address.

### Accounts and sign-in

The owner asked for a simple sign-up and login of our own, with the hashed credentials kept in a Hugging Face
dataset, instead of "Sign in with Hugging Face" (most invitees won't have an HF account). So:

#### Where accounts live

A third private dataset, `hf://datasets/jtouley/coffee-data-users`, holding two
append-only tables, `users` and `invites` (see Data model). Keeping accounts apart from the lake and the photos
means nothing that reads the lake (dbt, the MCP server, the weekly run) can see a password hash, and the token
the weekly run uses doesn't need access to it. The server loads both tables into memory at start and writes a new
record (one commit) for every change.

#### Passwords

Hashed with Argon2id (`argon2-cffi`, its default RFC 9106 low-memory parameters: 64 MiB, 3 passes,
4 lanes), with a per-hash random salt. Before hashing, the password is HMAC-ed with a pepper kept in Secret Manager
(`AUTH_PEPPER`), so a copy of the users dataset alone isn't enough to start guessing. Rules follow NIST 800-63B:
at least 10 characters, no composition rules, and a check against a short list of common passwords. Changing a
password writes a new `users` record.

#### Sign-up

Only with an invite code.

1. The owner taps "Invite someone" and gets a code like `K7QD-M2XF-9RPA-T4WE`: 80 random bits as 16 characters of Crockford base32 (digits
   and capitals without I, L, O and U; on input O reads as 0, I and L as 1, case and dashes don't matter), valid for
   7 days and usable once, and a link, `app.registry.coffee/join#K7QD-M2XF-9RPA-T4WE`. "Share link" opens
   Android's share sheet. Only the code's SHA-256 is stored, so it can't be shown again later; a pending invite
   offers "Send a new link", which revokes the old code and makes a new one. The code sits after `#`, so it never
   reaches server logs as part of the URL.
2. The invitee opens the link, lands on "jtouley invited you" with the code filled in, picks a username and a
   password, and is signed in. Typing the code by hand also works.
3. Bootstrapping the owner: when the `users` table is empty, the first sign-up needs `OWNER_SETUP_CODE`, a secret in
   Secret Manager, and creates the `owner` account. Each value of the secret works once: the server stores the SHA-256 of
   every setup code it has accepted, in the users dataset, and refuses a value it has seen. A setup code that has
   been used is inert, so leaving it in Secret Manager is no standing way into the owner's account.

#### Sign-in

Username and password. A failed attempt gets the same message whether the username exists or not, and
an unknown username is still checked against a dummy hash so the timing doesn't tell. Usernames are visible to
anyone who has been invited, so a lockout keyed on the username alone would let anyone keep the owner locked out.
Instead:

- Five failures for one username from one IP lock that pair for 15 minutes.
- Twenty failures from one IP lock that IP for 15 minutes.
- Failures for one username across all IPs only slow it down: each one doubles a delay before the next attempt is
  checked, from 1 s up to 30 s. They never lock it.

All of this is kept in memory; a restart clears it, which is acceptable at this size.

#### Sessions

No session table in the dataset (that would be a commit per login). The cookie is a signed token
(HMAC-SHA256 with the `SESSION_SECRET` secret) carrying `user_id`, `session_epoch` and the issue time. It is
`HttpOnly`, `Secure` and `SameSite=Lax`, lasts 90 days, and renews itself on use. Each `users` record has a
`session_epoch`. "Sign out everywhere", a password change and the owner disabling an account all bump it, which
invalidates every older cookie. Writes also need an `X-Requested-With` header, which a cross-site form can't send,
as CSRF protection on top of `SameSite`.

#### Forgotten passwords

There's no email, so the owner issues a reset code from the Invite screen. It works like an
invite but is tied to an existing account, and using it sets a new password and bumps the epoch. To reset the
owner's own password, the owner adds a new version of the `OWNER_SETUP_CODE` secret in Secret Manager (which proves
control of the Google Cloud project) and uses it once on the reset screen; as with setup, a value that has been used never works again.

#### Every request is scoped

Every write needs a signed-in account and touches only that account's data. The server reads `user_id` from the
cookie, never from the request body, and filters every read and write by it. The in-memory caches are keyed by
user. Tests cover a request with no session, or an expired or tampered one, trying each write route (rejected with
nothing written), and one user trying to read, correct or retract another user's shot, bag, photo or equipment.

Rejected: Sign in with Hugging Face (invitees would need HF accounts), Identity-Aware Proxy in front of Cloud Run (invitees would need Google accounts), passkeys only
(good, but more code to get right; worth adding later as a second way in), and magic links (need email).

### How writes reach the lake

Each action is one Hugging Face commit, made by the server with the existing `Lake.write` and `Lake.publish`:

- Sign-up, password change, invite: one commit each to the users dataset.
- New bag: two commits. First the photo's Parquet file to the photo dataset, then the `bags` row to the lake. If
  the second fails, the photo is orphaned but harmless, and the outbox retries the bag.
- Shot: one `shots` file.
- Equipment change: one `equipment` file.

`Lake.publish` already retries with backoff and treats files that landed on a lost response as uploaded. A commit
takes a second or two. The phone shows the saved screen immediately (the summary needs only the shot and data the server
already holds) and marks the shot as synced when the commit returns.

The phone generates `shot_id` and `bag_id` (UUIDs) before sending, and keeps each write in its outbox until the
server acknowledges it. The outbox sends a user's entries one at a time, in the order they were made. Three rules
keep retries from undoing anything:

- Every record carries `rev`, a counter the phone sets to one more than the `rev` of the version it last saw (1 for a
  new record). The server drops a write whose `rev` isn't greater than the stored one. So a save whose response was
  lost, resent after an Undo or a Correct, can't bring the old version back. `logged_at` is still stamped by the
  server, but it no longer decides between two versions from the phone.
- A resend identical to what's stored is acknowledged without writing (#13).
- File names are `<id>__<logged_at>-<6 random hex>.parquet` for every table, so two records for one id in the same
  second never collide. #13 does this for shots; equipment and bags need the suffix too (#22).

Each dataset (lake, photos, users) has its own staging folder (`build/lake-staging`, `build/photos-staging`,
`build/users-staging`), and `Lake.publish` uploads only that dataset's folder, one publish at a time per dataset,
under a lock. A shot publish can't carry a password hash or a photo into the main lake. A file that went up in
another request's commit counts as published, so a request never retries a commit that already succeeded.

The weekly run and the app can commit to the dataset at the same time: they touch different paths, and the
`concurrency: lake` group in Actions doesn't cover the app, so this relies on HF commits not conflicting on
disjoint files. The owner has approved one test during milestone 2: a commit from a test deployment to a test path
while a weekly run is committing.

### Where the bag photo is read

On the server, with the Anthropic key in Secret Manager. One request per photo: the image, a short instruction and
a JSON schema through structured outputs, so the response always parses. Bag labels are short but varied
(hand-lettered names, stickers on kraft paper, dates as "R 10.18" or "Roasted on 18/10").

The model is chosen by measurement, as the owner asked: Claude Opus 5.5 (`claude-opus-5-5`) and Claude Haiku 5.5
(`claude-haiku-5-5`) are compared on the same set of real bags before either becomes the default.

- The set: real bag photos with the right answer attached. The app builds this as it's used: every bag confirmed
  on the match card (or corrected through "Pick another match") is a photo with a known `coffee_id` and roast date. The
  first comparison runs on whatever bags exist when capture ships, plus any old bags or photos the owner has to
  hand, and it's re-run once there are 20. Hard labels (hand lettering, a sticker on kraft paper, a date stamp, a
  café's own bag) are worth adding on purpose.
- Until the comparison has 20 bags, Opus is the default, since it's the safer reader and costs about a cent a bag.
- Each model reads every photo three times at low effort, with the same prompt and schema.
- Scored per field: roaster, coffee name and roast date exact (after normalizing case and date format), plus the
  end-to-end result that matters: did the Python matcher land on the right `coffee_id`? Also logged: latency and
  cost per read, and whether the three runs agreed.
- Rule: use Haiku if it gets the same number of correct end-to-end matches as Opus (or misses only bags that Opus
  also struggles with) and its median latency is lower. Otherwise use Opus; at one bag a week the cost difference
  is under a dollar a year, so accuracy decides.
- The comparison is a script in the repo (`app/eval/bag_read.py`) with the photos in the private photo dataset, so
  it can be re-run whenever the prompt or the models change.

With Opus, the request turns on the API's server-side refusal fallback, so a declined read falls back to another
model instead of failing. Haiku 5.5 has no server-side fallback, so with Haiku a declined or failed read drops to
the manual path ("Type the coffee") and is logged.

The model only reads the label. Matching to the catalog stays deterministic, in Python, against `dim_coffee`; the
model never sees the catalog. That keeps the read cheap and the matching testable.

Rejected: reading on the phone (on-device OCR gets the text but not "which of these words is the roaster"), and
sending the catalog to the model (45,000 rows, and it would guess).

### Offline

Kitchen Wi-Fi is usually fine, but a shot should never be lost to a dropped connection.

- The app is a PWA with a service worker that caches the shell, so it opens offline.
- Every write goes through an outbox in IndexedDB and is retried until the server acknowledges the commit. The
  Today screen shows a small "2 waiting to sync" line when the outbox isn't empty. What each answer does to an
  entry:
  - 2xx: the entry is removed. This is the only answer that removes one silently.
  - No answer (offline, timeout, dropped connection), 408, 429 and any 5xx: the entry stays and is retried with
    backoff (from 2 s, doubling, up to 5 minutes), honouring `Retry-After` when the server sends it.
  - 401: the entry stays, and the app asks the person to sign in again; it's sent once they have.
  - Any other 4xx (the write can never succeed as sent, such as 400, 403, 404, 409 for a stale `rev`, or 422):
    the entry moves to a "Couldn't save" list on Today, with the server's message, where it can be fixed and resent

All new tables follow the existing pattern: one immutable Parquet file per record, latest record per id wins,
schemas in `lake.SCHEMAS`, globs in `lake.GLOBS` and `dbt/macros/lake.sql`, a zero-row schema file per table.

Every personal record carries a `user_id`: equipment, bags, photos and shots. Shots logged before accounts existed
have no `user_id`; dbt fills it with the owner's id (a dbt var, `owner_user_id`), so they stay the owner's. The
server applies the same rule when it loads shots, so a shot logged through the MCP server or the issue form shows up
for the owner straight away, not after the next weekly run. The MCP server and the issue form write `source` (`mcp`,
`issue`) and leave `user_id` empty.

## Privacy

- Bag photos stay private. They go to a separate private dataset, `hf://datasets/jtouley/coffee-data-photos`, as
  Parquet files in Hugging Face's `Image` layout, one photo per file. The main lake is private too, but a separate dataset means a
  mistake in the public export can't reach a photo, and the photos could be deleted wholesale without touching the
  lake's history. Only the `photo_id` is in the main lake.
- Why Parquet and not plain JPEG files: a Parquet photo goes through the same `Lake.write` and `Lake.publish` as every
  other record, and the image and its metadata (who, when, size, hash) are one immutable file that can't drift apart.
  Plain JPEGs would need a second write path for binary files and a separate metadata table kept in step with them.
- EXIF is removed on the phone before upload, so GPS coordinates of the kitchen never leave it. The server
  re-encodes the JPEG as a second check before writing the bytes into Parquet.
- Photos are served only through the app, to the user who took them, never by a direct HF URL. The server reads
  the `image` column and returns the bytes.
- Invited people's data lives in the owner's private datasets, so the owner can read it. The sign-up screen says so
  in one sentence. The app itself never shows one user another's data.
- Leaving. Retracting records hides them in the app and in dbt, but the lake is append-only and HF keeps file
  history, so a retraction isn't erasure. If an invitee asks for their data to be erased, the owner deletes their
  files from the three datasets and squashes the history (`HfApi.super_squash_history`). It's a manual
  exception to append-only, and it's the reason accounts and photos live in their own datasets: erasing them doesn't
  rewrite the catalog's history.
- Passwords never leave the server in plain text and are never logged. Request logging drops the body of the
  sign-in, sign-up and reset routes.
- The image goes to the Anthropic API to be read. Under standard API terms it isn't used for training; it is still
  a third party seeing a photo of a kitchen counter. The capture screen frames the bag tightly to keep the
  background small.
- Shots leave the public site. Today `site.py` renders "My shots: rating by brew ratio" and "Recent shots" from
  `fct_shot` on the GitHub Pages site; milestone 1 removes both sections and the scatter chart, and adds a test
  that the generated site contains no shot fields. Shots are then visible only in the app.
- The "Log a shot" issue form posts the shot and the reply as a GitHub issue, which is public if the repo is. #15
  kept it, since `suggest_next` still serves its replies. It stays until the app is live; then it comes off `main` and
  is kept on an archive branch, never deleted.

the milestone that builds it, and the test names the rule. A milestone isn't done until its rules' tests pass.

## Later: a dial-in model

The app doesn't suggest grind changes. The current rule ("sour or fast, go finer") is a rule of thumb, not something
learned from these shots, and a confident-looking suggestion from it would be wrong often enough to mislead. The
data the app collects is what a better suggestion needs: grind, dose, yield, time, taste, rating, grinder and the
bag's roast date.

Once a coffee has enough shots on one grinder (about 20), fit a small per-bag model of time and taste against grind,
dose and days off roast; a regression with a term per bag is enough to start. Compare it with the rule of thumb on
held-out shots: for each held-out shot, which one better predicted the time and taste of the next one? Show a
suggestion in the app only when the model reports its confidence and beats the rule of thumb on that test, and say
how sure it is ("Try 11. Likely 26 to 30 s.") instead of stating a single answer.

`shots.suggest_next` stays as it is for the MCP server and the issue-form replies.
